source: Snell's Law
n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with angles measured from the normal.
Students measure the angles from the surface instead of the normal.
When light crosses into a material with a different index of refraction at an angle, it bends. Snell's law gives the exact angle. You will undo a sine with inverse trig to find it.

$$\role[index of refraction, first medium]{constant}{n_1} \sin\role[angle in the first medium]{angle}{\theta_1} = \role[index of refraction, second medium]{constant}{n_2} \sin\role[angle in the second medium]{angle}{\theta_2},$$ with both angles measured from the normal. Going into a higher index, light bends toward the normal; going into a lower index, it bends away. Light that hits head-on ($\theta_1 = 0$) goes straight through.

Picture a row of marchers crossing from pavement into mud at a slant. The end that reaches the mud first slows down first, so the row swings around. Light's wavefronts do the same. In one period, the wavefront moves $\lambda_1$ in material 1 and $\lambda_2$ in material 2, and the two pieces share the same stretch $s$ of the boundary: $\lambda_1 = s\sin\theta_1$ and $\lambda_2 = s\sin\theta_2$. Divide: $\dfrac{\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_2} = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$, which is Snell's law.
A ray going from air into glass. The angles are marked from the dashed normal, not from the surface.

Measuring angles from the surface instead of from the normal. If a problem says the ray makes $25^\circ$ with the surface, the angle of incidence is $65^\circ$. Quick check: going into a denser material, your refracted angle (from the normal) must come out smaller than the incident angle.
Light in air hits water ($n = 1.33$) at $40^\circ$ from the normal. Find the angle of refraction.
Air into water
$\theta_2 = \sin^{-1}(0.483) = 28.9^\circ$. Smaller than $40^\circ$: it bent toward the normal.
Light in glass ($n = 1.50$) hits a boundary with water ($n = 1.33$) at $30^\circ$. Find the angle in the water.
Glass into water
$\theta_2 = 34.3^\circ$. Larger: going into a lower index, it bent away from the normal.
A ray enters a clear plastic from air at $50^\circ$ and travels at $31^\circ$ inside. Find the plastic's index.
Measuring an index
$n \approx 1.49$
$n_2 = \dfrac{n_1\sin\theta_1}{\sin\theta_2} = \dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{\sin 31^\circ}$.
